papers.title: Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Susan Harrington, Sonja Klein, Alice Catherine Fratoni, Charlott Sellberg, Oskar Lindwall
papers.abstract: Simulators have become central in professional training, in this case maritime education, where they support the development and assessment of skills and competencies required of competent seafarers. This study aims to inform the design of a learning analytics dashboard utilizing multimodal learning analytics to deliver automated, adaptive feedback to maritime students. Feedback is critical in simulator-based training, yet the characteristics of meaningful automated feedback in professional training remain underexplored. Drawing on a participatory design workshop with maritime students, the study examines tensions arising from the conceptualization of automated feedback. Using cultural historical activity theory, we frame tensions as opportunities for innovation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between students, instructors, and technology. In doing so, we offer insights into designing meaningful automated feedback for simulation training, and the need to balance students’ dual roles as learners and future professionals, reconciling collaborative learning with personalized feedback, and prioritizing educational goals over technological innovation.

papers.title: Raising Teachers’ Awareness to Embrace Diversity in Knowledge
papers.authors: Building
papers.abstract: Participating in Knowledge Building discourses for learners with visual impairments means that they can move from the current meritocratic and individual performance-based learning to ‘Currere,’ where they realize their existential meaning as members of society through others. This study compares the perspectives of special education teachers with those of general education teachers to promote inclusive Knowledge Building support through a mixed-methods case study, and analyzes the contradictions and tensions they currently face through Activity Theory.

papers.title: Collaboration and Competition in Educational Gameplay: Strategic Student Decision -Making
papers.authors: Tianyu Ma, Jennifer Kahn
papers.abstract: This study examines how middle school students engaged in strategic decision- making when collaboration and competition were tightly intertwined in an educational gameplay setting. Drawing from a design-based research study of an afterschool program, six students played Isles of Ilkmaar, a multiplayer game designed to support data science learning. Using Activity Theory as an analytic lens, we traced how students mobilized tools, interpreted rules, and negotiated roles in the game’s diner competition. Analysis of three gameplay episodes showed students adapting in real time, moving from tool learning to contested claims and finally to rule negotiation. Findings highlight that collaboration and competition were not separate modes of activity but operated together, with conflicts often catalyzing adaptation and role change. This work contributes to CSCL by showing how collaborative learning can be sustained under competitive pressures, offering implications for the design of educational environments that integrate both cooperative and adversarial elements.

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Activity Theory for Human-AI Teaming in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning
papers.authors: Jaeyoon Choi, Nia Nixon
papers.abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are reshaping the role of technology in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL). Once viewed as mediating tools, AI systems can now act as active teammates that co -construct meaning, share responsibility, and influence team cognition. This paper addresses the lack of theoretical grounding in existing human-AI teaming research by reconceptualizing Engeström’s Activity Theory. Specifically, we extend the six components of the activity system (subject, tool, rules, community, division of labor, and object) to account for AI’s dual role as both tool and quasi-subject within collaborative learning activities. Through this theoretical mapping, we highlight emerging questions for fut ure research, including but not limited to issues of learner agency, trust, equity, and epistemic alignment. We conclude with a call for the CSCL community to revisit and expand its theoretical frameworks to better capture the evolving dynamics of human-AI teaming.

papers.title: Belonging Infrastructure: A Designable Construct for Cultivating Teacher Agency in RPPs
papers.authors: Gregory Benedis-Grab, Alexandra Gendreau Chakarov
papers.abstract: Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) often rely on boundary infrastructure  to explain how collaboration is organized, but this lens overlooks how teacher agency is cultivated. We introduce belonging infrastructure, the designable features of collaboration that legitimize participant contributions and make belonging visible. Evidence from a teacher co -design workshop demonstrates how this construct provides a new lens for intentionally designing partnerships that foster teacher leadership, build district capacity, and expand who feels authorized to teach computer science.

papers.title: Calling, Collecting, and Transformation: Playful Artifacts as Pivots for Joint Activity and Game Design in a Collaborative VR Design Studio
papers.authors: Heliya Ahmadi, Xingxing Xie, Dylan Paré
papers.abstract: This paper examines how artifacts and environmental features mediate collaborative design in immersive VR. In a six- week VR collaborative studio, six designers co- created an LGBTQ+ mini-golf game. By triangulating video recordings with reflective journals, we found a stimulus -to-transformation design process that emerged from the perceptual noticing of collectibles, evolving into shared ideation and transforming game mechanics. Situated within activity theory, the study contributes process -oriented methods for researching collaborative VR design.

papers.title: Agency at Scale: Embedding Interpersonal Interaction and Collaboration
papers.authors: Montreal, Canada, June 10-15
papers.abstract: Responding to an increasing demand for scalability, designers have begun creating online teacher professional development (oTPD) platforms and curricula. However, researchers have also critiqued the field for overlooking the role of teacher voice and interpersonal interaction within the instructional design of most oTPD programs. In response, we explore the design and initial implementation of Zodiac, an online professional development platform specifically designed to amplify teacher agency within oTPD contexts through the application of activity theory. Using this tool, we developed and piloted a curri culum (called PathsPD) centered on helping teachers implement project -based learning in their classrooms and increasing learner-learner and learner-instructor interactions in online settings. In analyzing our design and post-interviews with users, we show that the technology/curriculum we developed attended to the community and division of labor aspects of the activity theory framework and amplified teacher choice and interpersonal interactions within this oTPD experience.

papers.title: Early Science Hub: Designing Interactive Simulations to Support Preschool Educators' Understanding of Science Core Ideas and Cross Cutting Concepts
papers.authors: Tiffany Leones, Danae Kamdar, Ximena Dominguez
papers.abstract: To support preschool educators’ integration of science in their classrooms, our project is co-designing the Early Science Hub (Hub), a professional learning resource based on promising components identified in prior work, with partner educators and curriculum/media designers. The Hub and its components are being designed to leverage technology and include educative features to make the resource widely accessible across early learning contexts. This paper details the design and iteration of one specific Hub component, the interactive simulations of science core ideas and cross cutting concepts designed to support preschool educators’ understanding of these. The session will invite participants to explore the interactive simulations and engage in a discussion to gather their insights and feedback, which can inform potential future iterations.

papers.title: Reimagining Literacy as Liberatory Learning: Centering Black Literacies in the Learning Sciences
papers.authors: Coco Massengale
papers.abstract: This paper outlines a research program situated at the intersection of the Learning Sciences, Literacy Studies, and Black Studies. The work investigates how racialized histories of literacy shape contemporary learning environments and how Black learners and communities design countercurricula that affirm joy, resistance, and self-determination. Drawing from archival, ethnographic, and design-based methods, this research advances a theoretical framework of bound literacy—a concept describing how literacy has historically been constrained by antiblackness—and explores what learning might look like when literacy is “unbound.” The program contributes to the Learning Sciences by positioning Black literacies as sites of innovation, imagination, and design, offering frameworks and methodologies for understanding learning as a collective, historical, and liberatory act. Overview My research bridges the Learning Sciences, Literacy Studies, and Black Studies to examine how racialized histories of literacy shape learning and how Black communities design liberatory literacies in response. This paper outlines my research program on “bound” and “unbound” literacies and its contributions to theorizing learning as a site of freedom-making. Theoretical framework: Learning as a liberatory and historical practice My research begins from the premise that learning is not only cognitive or social but also historical and political. Building on sociocultural theories of learning (e.g., Vygotsky, 1978) and critical traditions within the Learning Sciences (e.g., Nasir et al., 2006), I conceptualize literacy as a designed social practice shaped by structures of race, power, and history. To theorize this relationship, I introduced the framework of bound literacy (Massengale, 2024), which traces how literacy in the U.S. popular imagination has been historically “bound” to chattel slavery and its afterlives. This reframes literacy not as a neutral skill set but as a cultural construct used to delimit who counts as a learner. By examining how literacy has been racialized—particularly through associations with Black deficiency—this framework exposes how antiblackness has shaped the epistemological foundations of schooling, assessment, and learning theory. At the same time, I view literacy as a site of resistance and design. Across historical and contemporary contexts, Black people have cultivated literacies that imagine freedom beyond dominant educational systems. Aligning with Learning Sciences scholarship that centers imagination, equity, and design (e.g., Gutiérrez & Jurow, 2018), I argue that Black literacies are world-building practices that create new ways of being, knowing, and learning.

papers.title: Teaching and Learning Mathematics with Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Victoria Delaney
papers.abstract: Novel technologies influence the curriculum, pedagogy, and learning in schools. My research explores the impacts of AI-based tools in mathematics education, attending to how these tools influence teaching practice and how students learn to think mathematically. My scholarly goal is to support mathematics and stochastics teachers in developing innovative and robust pedagogies that uphold cognitive demand in learning even as tools that automate humanistic thinking become endemic to schooling. Overview My research centers curriculum, pedagogy, cognition, and AI/LLM automation in mathematics. I am interested in how AI-based tools mediate students’ mathematical thinking and teachers’ development of expert teaching practices to support student thinking. My interests stem from my experience as a high school math teacher of seven years, where I learned that mathematics tools and curricular resources played a major role in lesson orchestration and what my students ultimately learned (Brown, 2011). I conceptualize teachers and learners as agentic, creative, and curious drivers of learning rather than recipients of societal changes influenced by developments in AI automation. I further envision teachers as lesson designers and orchestrators who, when faced with the latest technological disruptions, can design effective instruction based in part on multi-faceted forms of teacher knowledge, including knowledge of how students’ interactions with tools impact their learning. To support teacher learning with insights about AI-tools’ impacts on students’ mathematical thinking, I have recently begun to research students’ AI-mediated problem solving processes (Delaney et al., 2025b). This work is in its second year and involves both well-defined and ill-defined mathematics tasks. I conduct video- recorded task-based interviews and observe the problem solving processes that surround students’ decisions, evaluations, AI trust, and epistemic judgments of mathematics output produced by chatbots. I have initiated this work in both clinical and classroom settings with algebra, calculus, statistics, data science, and numerical reasoning tasks. The findings from these studies inform my own teaching practice and AI adaptations, and with this knowledge, I continuously work to help other teachers develop design skills for an AI-integrated future. Establishing this program requires proficiency with the latest technologies. Under some conditions, technologies can create dynamic, inquiry-driven learning experiences that raise the cognitive demand required to solve nonroutine tasks, such as appraising the quality of a dataset or designing a facial recognition classifier (Delaney & Lee, 2024; Delaney & Selbach-Allen, 2025). In other circumstances, technology can derail students (or teachers) from their learning goals. My research program explores how teachers and students use novel technologies, the affordances and challenges that arise from their technology use, transformations on student and teacher thinking that are mediated by technology, and implications for learning. Theoretical frameworks I draw from theoretical frameworks that foreground the complexity of teaching and learning. I have several lines of research that build from different lineages of theory. When I conceptualize relationships between math curriculum and teaching, I draw from Brown’s illustration of teaching as adaptative, improvisational design work, akin to orchestrating a jazz concert (Brown, 2011). His pedagogical design capacity framework formed the basis of my dissertation, where I studied how statistics teachers adapted and enacted a machine learning curriculum (Delaney, 2025). When I conceptualize teachers’ mathematical professional learning with AI, I draw from teacher knowledge (Shulman, 1986) and teacher noticing (van Es & Sherin, 2008). What teachers attend to, interpret, and how they respond to students is directly related to their knowledge. Yet while teachers are still in the early stages of developing their knowledge, they may not yet have the multimodal forms of expertise to evaluate LLMs’ output and/or claims about students’ mathematical thinking. I am therefore developing theories about when and how mathematics teachers may prompt LLMs as cognitive supports, and what additional (human) supports they need to grow their pedagogical content knowledge and noticing abilities. From the student perspective, I have recently explored knowledge building with AI-based tools (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2020) and building expertise in mathematics with LLMs (Chi & Glaser 1985; Hiebert & Carpenter, 1992). Today’s LLMs can imitate humanistic mathematical reasoning, and can complete most of K- 12 mathematics tasks with minimal prompting specifications. It is therefore necessary for students and teachers to discern how to use LLMs to build knowledge and foster their own expertise rather than bypass the cognitive work involved in mathematics problem solving altogether. Recent work has begun to explore what human learning a nd epistemic agency may look like when LLMs are involved in mathematics tasks, proposing that students’ uses of LLMs are indicative of how much problem solving agency they retain versus offload to intelligent agents (Wu et al., 2025). I intend to extend this work and study how students’ LLM uses mediate their moment-by-moment thinking and what agency they preserve as they develop problem solving skills.

papers.title: Creating Thirdspace: Indigenous Learning Lab for Survivance
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Aydin Bal
papers.abstract: Racialization of school discipline is an enduring systemic problem in the United States. This formative intervention study is based on a collaboration with 14 school stakeholders: American Indian students, parents, community members, and educators at a rural high school in a community- driven problem-solving process called Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL). Members analyzed the root causes of the racialized school discipline and created a new behavioral support system. Utilizing critical geography and decolonizing methodology, this formative intervention study aimed to unpack how ILL members formed Thirdspace —a space of resistance, possibilities, and hopes —to address enduring racial disproportionality in school discipline. Members challenged race- neutral representations of space, mapped out dystopia, revitalized American Indian epistemology, and mapped out a real utopian vision of schooling. Racialization of school discipline in the U.S The U.S. school system has been a settler -colonial space since its inception, in which First Nations students and families struggle over cultural and linguistic erasure, recognition, and educational sovereignty (Grande, 2015; Lomawaima & McCarty, 2006; Sab zalian, 2019; Wolfe, 2006). Indigenous ontologies, epistemologies, morals, and educational practice were/are pathologized by the settler -colonial state (Lomawaima & McCarty, 2006). School discipline has historically been a tool for the settler projects of forced assimilation and cultural genocide masqueraded as “education.” American Indian youth experience multiple forms of marginalization in the settler - colonial school system. Particularly, exclusionary school discipline (e.g., out -of-school suspension, expulsion, and referrals to law enforcement) has been used as a tool of exclusion through which Indigenous bodies are erased from the learning space and white settler-colonial privilege and property are reinforced and perpetuated. Despite complexity in disproportionality patterns across states, districts, and schools, nationally American Indian students are more likely to receive frequent and harsher school discipline compared to their white counterparts (Whitford et al., 2019). Racial disproportionality is a byproduct of settler-colonial practices that spatially arrange geography of opportunity (Tate, 2008) based on racial lines and is also a tool of erasure to uphold settler -colonial power privileging whiteness over indigeneity. To disrupt the racialized school discipline system, it is imperative to investigate how power, privilege, and marginalization are indexed in local social, spatial, and historical contexts simultaneously (Soja, 2010; Tuck & McKenzie, 2015). To address settler -colonial violence embedded in disciplinary policies and practices, a formative intervention, Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL), was implemented in a close collaboration with an Anishinaabe Tribal government at Newhope High School (NHS) (Pseudonyms for all name of places and people in this paper) in a Midwest state between 2019 and 2024. As a community participatory design project, the ILL facilitated a critical design praxis of local school stakeholders —i.e., reflecting on systemic tensions a nd contradictions entrenched in the existing school system and taking collective action to co-design locally meaningful solutions in response to the needs, goals, and visions of school stakeholders ( Afacan et al., 2021; Ko et al., 2022; Ko et al., 2023). The ILL was a systemic transformation through an inclusive problem -solving space that centered  the multiple voices, perspectives, and histories of American Indian students and families, who together with school professionals designed  a new school behavioral  support system that reflected  Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies (Ko et al., 2023). This study documents how ILL members leveraged their individual and collective histories and experiences in a dialogic space to disrupt: The settler -colonial school space that is socially, historically, spatially, and politically constructed to uphold white power and privilege; and color neutral and technocratic diagnosis of and solutions to racial disparities in behavioral and academic outcomes. Through the ILL, part icipants, in particular Anishinaabe members, formed Thirdspace —a generative space filled with survivance, transgression, and new imaginations (hooks, 1989; Soja, 1996; Vizenor, 2008). 570 Theoretical framework To address racial disproportionality within social-spatial-historical contexts of settler colonialism in the Anishinaabe nation, this study was epistemologically grounded in cultural historical activity theory (CHAT) to racial disproportionality in school discipline stemming from the intellectual legacy of Vygotsky and social constructivism (1993; 1978). CHAT positions learning and human development as inseparable from the social, historical, and geographical contexts where people learn and develop as participants of multiple cultural activity systems such as family, community, and education professionals (Engeström, 2016; Rogoff, 2003). CHAT considers social, historical, and spatial underpinnings that materialize in the form of cultural tools used in disciplinary processes (e.g., a school’s behavioral expectations, rules about referral processes, personnel involved in the process, artifacts, and division of labor). Within the cultural -historical approach, racial disproportionality is a byproduct of systemic discrimination: both a result and tool that sustains settler colonial power (Lomawaima & McCarty, 2006 ). The overrepresentation of American Indian students in discipline is inseparable from the historical landscape of settler colonialism materialized in day -to-day and institutional interactions, such as the struggle over land and water, and Indigenous sovereignty. Coupled with the cultural-historical approach to racial disproportionality, this study centered Indigenous educational sovereignty through an interdisciplinary epistemological grounding informed by decolonization theory (Brayboy, 2005; Tuck & McKenzie, 2015) and critical geography (Lefebvre, 1991; Soja, 1996; Velez & Solórzano, 2017). The cross -pollination of these frameworks is powerful to investigate how settler colonialism historically produces and perpetuates racialized space through everyday schooling practices. This theoretical synthesis helped identify how Indigenous local stakeholders exercised their transformative agency to explore the new spatial possibility of resistance and sovereignty represented by the systemic design process. Thirdspace We utilized the thinking  of Henri Lefebvre (1991) and Edward Soja (1996)  to establish the basis of critical geography, specifically the concept of Thirdspace. Lefebvre's  trialectical relations of space, which encompass perceived and lived spaces, serve as a foundation for understanding of Thirdspace as a hybrid space with radical openness. Perceived space, also known as spatial practice (Lefebvre, 1991) or Firstspace (Soja, 1996), refers to the tangible, everyday environments that individuals experience through their senses, such as parks, schools, and sidewalks. These spaces are often taken for granted and shaped by social technocrats, such as urban designers and policymakers. Conceived space, also referred to as representations of space (Lefebvre, 1991) or Secondspace (Soja, 1996), encompasses the conceptual imagination of space by those in positions of power, such as architects and planners or school policy makers who design and assign space based on their expertise and knowledge. This creates orders that users of space typically accept without much resistance, as exemplified by the physical layout of schools or cities, and the proximity of reservations to educational resources. The l ived space (Lefebvre, 1991) or Thirdspace (Soja, 1996), is the mental imagination in physical space. It is the space of sense-making. The lived space encompasses the perceived and the conceived space yet simultaneously transcends them. Soja, building upon Lefebvre’s spatial trialectics, situated Lefebvre’s lived space or spaces of representation as a hybrid space (Bhabha, 1994); a gold mine of counter space where “…resistance to the dominant order arising precisely from their subordinate, peripheral or marginalized positioning” (Soja, 1996 p. 68). This counter space is what Soja termed Thirdspace. Tribal epistemology We paired the concept of Thirdspace with TribalCrit. TribalCrit recognizes the liminality of American Indian students and families as well as their historical and everyday challenges to settler -colonial practices. Resistance to settler-colonialism may create emancipatory space or the Thirdspace of sovereignt y that transcends control over lands (Bruyneel, 2007). Sovereignty is a dialectical relationship between resistance and place: “The ability of a group of people to make their own decisions and control their own lives in relation to the space where they reside and/or that they envision as their own” (Bruyneel, 2007, p. 23). The Thirdspace of sovereignty surpasses the dichotomy of colonial binary rules: Indigenous people’s location as inside or outside of the system. Given the context of the Newhope community, in this paper, we document how ILL members leveraged their individual and collective agency utilizing their lived experiences embedded in their specific socio- spatial-historical context to form Thirdspace, within which they challenged the existing settler colonial power and privilege embedded within school disciplinary policies and practices and designed a locally meaningful school level behavioral support system. 571 The present study Socio-spatial-historical contexts of Newhope High School American Indian students in NHS are overrepresented in exclusionary disciplines. In the 2019- 2020 school year in which this study occurred, NHS’s enrollment was 70.6% white, 21% American Indian, 3.2% Latine, 1% Asian, 0.1% Black or African American, and 3.7 % from two or more races (Department of Public Instruction, 2020). While American Indian students constituted one-fifth of the student enrollment, they received 64.3% of in-school suspensions and 62.8% of out-of-school suspensions (Newhope High School Discipline Data, 2019). What are visible as school discipline problems in NHS have socio- spatial-historical roots that are undetachable from Indigenous, in this case the Anishinaabe’s struggle over rights to space, ancestral land, control and exercise of treaty rights, political autonomy, economic -self-sufficiency and a desire to revive and preserve cultural heritage; struggle over recognition and control over one’s own life (Silvern, 1995). The Newhope region itself is often known as the “deep north”. In the 1980s, NHS and the city of Newhope was the epicenter of an anti- Indian movement known as the “Walleye War”, triggered by treaty rights dispute (Nesper, 2002). White protestors chanted slogans such as “ Save a walleye, spear an Indian” during protests at boat landings at lakes where the Anishinaabe spearfish. The Anishinaabe community members risked their lives fishing. The dysfunctional socio- spatial-historical climate at the community level accumulated to deep distrust and broken relationships between Natives and non-Natives at NHS. Grounded in the socio-spatial-historical context of Newhope, this paper is aimed to investigate how the ILL members centered the racialized day -to-day and institutional experiences within and outside of school in their collective efforts to create a new culturally responsive behavioral support system.

papers.title: A Case Study of Activity Structures and Resources that Support Teacher Agency and Leadership in an RPP
papers.authors: Kelly Billings, UC Berkeley, Marcia C. Linn
papers.abstract: This case study reveals how one teacher’s agency and leadership in a Research Practice Partnership (RPP) impacted the design of a justice- centered science unit. We analyze RPP documents and data, from design meetings, workshop transcripts, observations, a nd informal co-design conversations, to reveal the ways RPP activity structures helped to support the teachers’ leadership. We report our findings in three illustrative episodes. Episode 1 reveals how the teachers’ longstanding involvement with the RPP empowered him to bring a new unit topic to the collaboration. Episode 2 documents the teachers’ leadership during workshops. Episode 3 reveals how conversations between the teacher and the learning scientist during unit implementation supported the refinement of the unit and reflection on teaching practice.

papers.title: Developing Relational Agency for Addressing Racialization of School Discipline in the U.S
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Dosun Ko, Aydin Bal, Linda Orie, Elizabeth Schrader, Jahyun Yoo, Morgan Mayer-Jochimsen
papers.abstract: In this paper, we adapt Edwards's (2005; 2007) concept of relational agency, situating it within the context of racialized schooling in the U.S. We posit that the ability to recognize and leverage others' support in addressing a complex problem necessitate s the ability to acknowledge the historical legacies of systemic racial violence ingrained in everyday school practices. To support our theoretical argument, we present a case from Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL), an inclusive task force established to design a culturally responsive behavioral support system addressing racial disproportionality in school discipline in a predominantly white high school serving American Indian students. Specifically, we emphasize the relational agency of Mr. Archer, the school principal, as he worked together with ILL members, particularly American Indian members. The purpose of this paper is to explore how a diverse group of local stakeholders developed relational agency (Edwards, 2005; 2007) while collaborating on the Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL) project. The project aimed to create a culturally responsive school  behavioral support system addressing racial disproportionality in school disciplinary practices at Newhope High School (NHS) (Pseudonym) in rural Wisconsin in the U.S., serving American Indian students. The ILL was an inclusive problem -solving task force where members collectively address local systemic social injustice issues (Bal et al., 2018). The ILL was comprised of members from diverse roles (e.g., parents, students, community members, educators, administrators) and racial/ethnic groups. This diverse group collaborated, recognized, and utilized each other’s socio- spatial-historical perspectives and lived experiences as legitimate sources of knowledge. This collaborative approach allowed members to collectively unpack the complex problem of racial disproportionality in school discipline and proposed solutions tailored to their localized contexts. This paper specifically examines the relational agency of one member, Mr. Kevin Archer (Pseudonym), the principal at NHS, as he learned and developed his agency through interactions and engagements with other ILL members. Investigating Mr. Archer’s relational agency is critical because the creation of school discipli ne policies/system is typically perceived as the domain of school technocrats, including principals and other members of administration at the school or district level. Administrators, like Mr. Archer, possess the privilege and authority to make decisions regarding the school system. Hence, it is crucial to understand how individuals with power and privilege utilize these attributes to learn from other stakeholders, particularly parents, community members, and historically marginalized students to collectively create systemic changes. This paper is theoretically anchored in the framework of relational agency (Edwards, 2005; 2007), which emphasizes how a group of professionals across boundaries of practice work together to solve a complex problem. In the context of the U.S education system, embedded within a history of discrimination and oppression, we argue that the framework of relational agency needs expansion to capture the historical -social-spatial-political nuances that diverse groups of people bring to the table as they collaborate. The overarching question guiding this study is: How did the school principal develop relational agency throughout ILL? Racialization of school disciplinary practices The racialization of discipline in U.S. schools remains a persistent civil rights issue, with Black and American Indian/Alaska Native students experiencing the highest percentages of out -of-school suspensions in public K -12 schools (Leung-Gagné et al., 2022). Overrepresentation of historically marginalized students in school discipline is not merely an individual issue of students’ incapability to follow school norms. It is also not simply attributed to educators’ biases in singling out certain students based on their racial groups. We argue that racial disproportionality is a manifestation of how discipline systems—including norms and the roles of administrators and educators themselves—are embedded within whiteness and are permeated by day- to-day interactions within and outside of the school environment. The racialization of school discipline is fundamentally a form of violence 722 against Black and Brown students, justified through disciplinary measures. The long- term impacts include the negative stigma associated with the criminalization of Black and Brown bodies and the loss of instructional time (Losen & Martinez, 2020), among other consequences. For American Indian students and families, historical practices, such as massacres, forced relocations away from native territories, the devastating impacts of boarding schools (Lewis et al., 2021), forced assimilations, and numerous broken federal treaties  mark the dispossession of indigeneity. In the contemporary context, even without the presence of boarding schools, the settler-colonial education system continues to function as a tool for the dispossession of American Indian sovereignty (Lomawaima & McCarty, 2006). In the school year 2017- 18 alone, American Indian/Alaskan Native students were suspended more often than the national average, with a rate of 7% compared to the overall average of 5% (Leung -Gagné et al., 2022). The current settler-colonial education system persistently marginalizes American Indian students through disciplinary practices. Local policy reform from the ground-up Given the nature and complexity of racial disproportionality embedded in the structure of oppression and discrimination, it is imperative for local stakeholders to work together  in addressing this complex issue. Top - down policy initiatives miss the complex nuance of how historically marginalized students and families experience racial disproportionality on a daily basis. School administrators’ ontological and epistemological understanding, as well as their approach to address racial disproportionality might differ from those of the students and families from historically marginalized backgrounds. Therefore, boundary-crossing efforts that bring multiple stakeholders with various roles and responsibilities to work together to collaboratively address a complex problem is imperative (Akkerman & Baker, 2011; Ko et al., 2021; Edwards, 2020). Despite multiple policy reforms, local school policies that co -design school discipline systems with— rather than for—historically marginalized students and families remain rare (Penuel, 2019). Although efforts, in the form of Multi -Tiered Support Systems (MTSS), have been made to co -design with students and families, transformative changes are still lacking. A similar injustice occurs in other racially contested education systems such as special education, where historically marginalized students are also o verrepresented in disability categories. The lack of co -design with historically marginalized students and families is far from an act of distributed expertise between school and family, it ignores and further exacerbates the racialized system of special education that perceives historically marginalized families as incapable of co-designing policies that impact their lives. Theoretical framework This paper is grounded in the theoretical concept of relational agency (Edwards, 2005; 2007). Relational agency is action with others through which to recognize others as resources for collaborative problem-solving and crafting new tools and practices (Edwards, 2005, 2007). Relational agency transcends mere collaborative efforts. Instead, it signifies a capability to identify, actively seek and offer supports as well as effectively employ the support of others as valuable assets to transform an existing system (Edwards, 2005; 2007). In CHAT terms, relational agency is capacity to work with others to expand the object that one is working on and trying to transform by recognising and accessing the resources that others bring to bear as they interpret and respond to the object. It is a capacity which involves recognising that another person may be a resource and that work needs to be done to elicit, recognise and negotiate the use of that resource in order to align oneself in joint action on the object. It offers an enhanced version of pe rsonal agency and as a capacity it can be learnt. (Edwards, 2005, p. 172) From the cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) viewpoint, racial disproportionality in school discipline is a manifestation of historically accumulated and ongoing systemic contradictions that are embedded in settler colonialism, institutional racism and ableism, and structural inequities. This systemic injustice is intersectional and extends beyond a single activity system. Building on the original concept of relational agency, in this paper, we offer and expansion Edward’s concept to the context of racialized school disciplinary practices in the U.S. We acknowledge the capacity to recognize and utilize other stakeholder’s knowledge as an imperative in boundary crossing. However, in the context of racialized and politicized education system in the U.S., those characteristics requires further adaptation. We argue that the capacity to “recognize” other people as resources necessitates the ability to acknowledge the historical legacies of educational debt and systemic racial violence persisting within everyday school practices, including disciplinary practices, both in the past and the present (Kramarczuk Voulgarides, 2023; Ladson-Billings, 2006). Stakeholders' ability to recognize historical legacies of systemic oppression in school 723 disciplinary practices will manifest in their capacity to draw upon historical accounts and interpretations of systemic oppression and racism when collaboratively addressing complex problems like racial disproportionality in school discipline. This, in turn, informs stakeholders —especially those trained to operate within bureaucratic technicalities, such as school administrators— in their interpretation and approaches when making sense of racial disproportionality in their localized socio -spatial-historical contexts. Furthermore, the capacity to “recognize” entails acknowledging that historically marginalized students and families, including American Indian and Black students and their families, have endured and persevered in the face of systemic oppression (Brayboy, 2005). Therefore, they possess legitimate knowledge to co- create solutions to the perennial issue. By recognizing the intricate socio-spatial-historical contexts contributing to racially disparate disciplinary outcomes for historically marginalized students, it opens the possibility for diverse stakeholders to actively seek out various perspectives, particularly those of historically marginalized students and their families. Second, we argue that in relational agency, the capacity to utilize other stakeholders' perspectives, knowledge, and empirical experiences, especially those from historically marginalized backgrounds, requires the ability to place historically marginalized  students, families, and community members at the forefront of local school policy reforms as experts in their own experiences (i.e., the racialized experience of school discipline). In boundary crossing work, each stakeholder enters the collaboration with  diverse ways of looking at the problem, in this case, racial disproportionality. Because their motives differ, each member naturally has a unique understanding of racial disproportionality and contributions to finding solutions to the problem. In summary,  we argue that the capacity to work together requires stakeholders, particularly those with privilege and power to determine the school system, to recognize the education system as embedded within a larger system of oppression and discrimination and to center the voice and values of historically marginalized students and families in the local level reform efforts. Current study: Relational agency in ILL Data collection and analysis Mr. Archer, who is the main focus  of the boundary -crossing actor in this paper, showing the development of relational agency, identified himself as a white male. At the time of the ILL project, Mr. Archer had been working at NHS for over 10 years in various roles. He held the role of principal just before this project began. We utilized ethnographic data collected during the design phase of the ILL that took place from the 2019/20 academic year as the data for this paper. The ILL was comprised of 14 school stakeholders embodying multiple r oles and demographic backgrounds (e.g., three parents/community members, five educators, three students, and three administrators). ILL members met monthly for a duration of one hour and 30 minutes. ILL sessions were guided by a cycle of systemic change (Engeström, 2008) (See figure 1). For this paper, our primary data consists of video transcripts of the recorded meetings. The analytic approach of this study followed abductive process, characterized by iterative movement between theory and data for the purpose of theory building (Tavory & Timmermans, 2014). Initially, we applied Edwards’ original concept of relational agency to make sense of the data. Upon thorough examination, we observed an expanded form of agency among ILL members. Subsequently, we revisited the theoretical framework and adapted Edwards' model to align with this racialized and politicized educational context, and as commonly found in the U.S. Utilizing this expanded framework, detailed in the theoretical framework section, we reanalyzed the data and discuss our findings in this paper. During the data analysis process, we were not able to conduct member checking with principal Archer. Context Within NHS, American Indian students were disproportionately represented in school disciplinary actions. While they accounted for about 20% of the student population, they received 64.3% of in-school suspensions and 52.2% of out-of-school suspensions (Wisc onsin Department of Public Instruction, 2019). Racial disproportionality in NHS has its roots in the social-geographical-historical-political contexts of Newhope, a place known as the “Deep North.” The city of Newhope was the epicenter of anti-Indian movements and anti-spearfishing protests that took place in Wisconsin during the 1980s and early 1990s (Nesper, 2002). Despite state and federal court affirmations of the Ojibwe treaty rights, which granted Tribal people the right to harvest fish in their ceded lands, the community has a memory and lived experience of racism, exclusion, prejudice, and hostility between Indigenous and White residents. The settler colonial tensions are still visible in Newhope today through multiple community conflicts. Figure 1 Expansive Learning Cycle guiding ILL Process 724 Findings This analysis centers on the demonstrated relational agency of Mr. Archer, the principal of NHS, as he actively engaged in inclusive and democratic dialogues within the Indigenous Systemic Change Lab (ILL). Our findings suggest that Mr. Archer's relational agency, focusing on understanding root causes of racial disproportionality, is closely linked to his gradual shift in perspectives. Specifically, Mr. Archer evolved from viewing school discipline and behavioral achievement as neutral information to adopting a perspective rooted in the socio- spatial historical understanding of discipline within the framework of settler colonial practices. Neutrality in understanding data and American Indian students’ educational experience In the first ILL session, Mr. Archer presented NHS data on academic outcomes, represented by students’ American College Testing (ACT) score, a standardized test used to measure college readiness in the U.S. The data served as a stimulus for ILL  members to understand the here and now problem of school discipline at NHS. In his presentation, Mr. Archer boasted about NHS’ academic achievement at the regional and state level assuming neutrality of data: Our test results versus the state average ACT composite average scores have been compared very well with the state averages over the years. Last year, 17-18, our composite scores were better than anybody in our Athletic Conference, and the second best in the entire region which includes all the [Lakewood] schools. Hit a little dip last year but still, as you can see, our line is the blue line, still better than State average by quite a bit. Here's a little chart that shows our students readiness for meeting college benchmarks, for the ACT versus State average. The last couple years we've made some ground up and now we’re outdistancing the state in that regard. (ILL #1) Here, Mr. Archer was unable to relate to the context of settler-educational practices. He looked at the data in neutral way. However, at the end of the data presentation, Ms. Diana Prince, an Ojibwe community member, challenged the assumed neutrality of data. Diana Prince: Do you have this broken down by the feeder schools? Kevin Archer: No. We could, I suppose, Diana. We could go back in and add in hoc groups for students that came to us from [the six feeder K-8 schools]. NHS received students from six K -8 schools. Of those schools, five were  predominantly white, and the Tribal school located in the Ojibwe reservation was  predominantly American Indian (with about 90% enrollment). Examining students’ academic achievement based on their feeder school might provide a more nuanced picture 725 of academic outcomes. We argue that Mr. Archer’s response to Ms. Prince was a germ cell for relational agency. He was receptive to the constructive criticism raised by other ILL  members, particularly Ojibwe members. However, he was not able to relate to the socio- spatial-historical contexts of learning in NHS. Mr. Archer continued with a presentation of academic achievement based on students’ racial groups and again expressed pride that NHS’ ACT scores remain the highest in northern Wisconsin and the state. After presenting the academic data, part of engaging in the questioning section (See figure 1), Mr. Archer also presented NHS’s behavior data. Here, Ms. Prince, continued challenging the assumed neutrality of data: Kevin Archer:  This is a report that we always run the top five most occurring discipline referrals in our school. Our disappointing referral system that we have in place, 197 students in our school that had one or more disciplinary referrals, this is last year's numbers, 100 with two or more, 57 with three or more, so there are obviously some students who are repeatedly being referred to the office for multiple times by multiple teachers. But we always encourage our folks engage in a referral process because typically at least more than half the time the first discipline referral is the only one that student experienced. Diana:    About how many of those are Native students? Kevin Archer: You know, I didn't break that slide down. Mr. Archer continued presenting school discipline at the intersection of special education. Kevin Archer:  This is another slide that compares those all students and Native American students, students with IEPs and disciplinary referrals that have to do with threatening behavior, aggression, or harassment. It's kind of a wide web there. A lot of different behaviors can fall into those categories. Diana:   I don’t understand why you don’t have this broken down by non- native students, also. I’m trying to sit here and do the math on red is native students and blue is all students so how much the non-native students are. Kevin Archer:  I only broke it down to native because that's what [the facilitators] requested. Diana:   Well, that’s what we’re looking at right? It would be beneficial if you put the non- native students also so that we could compare all students. Here, Ms. Prince crossed the perceived boundary of “expertise” in looking at data and utilized her experience and perspectives as a community member, a parent, and a former student of NHS to request the principal to present the school’s discipline data disaggregated by race for all racial/ethnic groups, not just for American Indian students, to see the distribution of causes of disciplinary referrals across racial/ethnic groups. Mr. Archer was open to a democratic dialogue with Ms. Prince. He was able to li sten to Ms. Prince and allow more room for her to bring her critical perspectives on looking at data, challenging the masquerade of data. The ILL members then agreed to have Mr. Archer present disaggregated data in the next meeting. In this first ILL  session, Mr. Archer’s germ cell of relational agency was visible through his capacity to engage in democratic dialogue with Ms. Prince. While Mr. Archer did not fully develop a critical stance in examining academic and behavioral achievement, his capability to open up room for Ms. Prince to center her critical perspectives and lived experiences as an Indigenous member grounded in racialization of education into data meaning-making was a germ-cell of developing relational agency. From race-neutrality to a germ cell of relational agency The questioning of data continued in the second ILL session, particularly focusing on suspension data. This time, Mr. Archer built on Ms. Prince’s suggestion from the first ILL session present disaggregated data comparing American Indian and white students. When analyzing discipline data by race/ethnic group, it was clear that American Indian students were grossly overrepresented in suspensions. The ILL members examined the 2016/17- , 2017/18- , and 2018/19- year data. In 2016, American Indian students were 60% in the school’s suspension incidents while comprising of only 20% of the total school population. In 2017, American Indian students were 48% of the total incidents. And, in 2018, they were 47% percent of the total number of suspension incidents while comprising of only one -fifth of the total school population. By examining data disaggregated by race, Principal Archer gradually developed his capacity to:1) Draw from other members suggestions to interpret data, and; 2) move from perceiving NHS as the best school for all students including American Indian students to acknowledging racialized practices in the school disciplinary practice. He stated: 726 This slide is a talking point and a conundrum for me. Maybe this group over the course of the next year can help me figure out why. But when I look at the disproportionality in the suspensions, that’s bad news for me. That’s like we’re in a bad place. That’s got to change and that’s awful. When I see the academic piece, it doesn't jive with the same message I get when I read the last few slides. I don’t claim to have the answer.  Why is it that academically, we’re outperforming the snot out of a lot of the schools in the state to have really similar, if not exactly the same, demographics. (ILL #2) In the second ILL session, with disaggregated data presented, and perhaps fueled by the democratic dialogue in the previous ILL session, Mr. Archer continued to exercise his relational agency. He started to develop a critical stance that NHS was not a race-neutral place. Mr. Archer's humility to center the struggle, perspectives, and lived experiences of the Ojibwe students and families mediated more democratic dialogue among ILL  members, opening the way for further centering of the lived experiences of Ojibwe students and families within the context of the racialization of academic and behavioral outcomes. Ms. Lola:  Are those the ACT scores of just the Native students? Mr. Archer:   No, this is the ACT score of every kid and every one of those high schools. Mr. Black:  Cumulative? Mr. Archer:  Yes. Mr. Jeremiah:  I think we had that conversation of the Native kids being absorbed into the demographics that come in percentages. I’m not saying it's a false reading, but you got to pull Native kids out of that and have another bar there saying where the native kids fall  into that because personally, I've seen some of the kids sat in on some of the testing and it's not their cup of tea. (ILL #2) Here, Mr. Jeremiah, NHS’s American Indian educator, joined Ms. Diana Prince to challenge the perceived neutrality of examining quantitative data. Mr. Jeremiah juxtaposed the numerical data with the lived day- to-day educational experiences of American Indian students in NHS. Challenging the assumed neutrality of the educational environment of NHS resulted in a more nuanced understanding of the experiences of American Indian students in NHS. This paradigm shift represented evolving learning from Principal Archer, who transitioned over the course of ILL  from a race-neutral stance to embracing politicized solidarity and engaging in genuine racial dialogue with Ojibwe members (Vakil et al., 2016). Here, Mr. Archer moved from a germ cell to a sprout of relational agency. In the thir d ILL session, Mr. Archer indicated more learning and growth of his relational agency, utilizing a critical stance when examining data. For me personally, when I started to break the data down by ethnicity, I was about ready to jump off the ledge when I saw the difference. And then when I looked at our Native students versus non-Native students at these other schools in the country, now I feel so bad. (ILL #3) Here, Mr. Archer signaled a change in perspectives about the experience of American Indian students. We argue that Mr. Archer was able to recognize the racialization of school disciplinary practices and acknowledge that the school, NHS, was not a race- neutral place. In the fifth ILL meeting, Mr. Archer acknowledged that NHS was “a rough place for a Native American student to be a student.” Developing strong relational agency In the fifth session of the ILL, where members engaged in the modeling process (See Figure 1), Mr. Archer invited all ILL members to look back at the school’s history of the expulsion of American Indian students in NHS. It is important to note that Mr. Archer voluntarily decided to explore the school discipline data from 20 years ago. We argue that Mr. Archer’s decision to examine the pattern of expulsion, grounded in the history of coloniality materialized in the dispute of treaty rights between the Indige nous Ojibwe community and the local white community (re: Walleye war) in the late 1980s, was an indicator of learning and further expansion of his relational agency. Mr. Archer developed his relational agency to work with the ILL members by situating the root causes of disciplinary practices within the socio -spatial-historical contexts of NHS and Newhope as an embodiment of settler-colonialism and coloniality. Mr. Archer shared his historical understanding of data in the fifth meeting. While the illustrativ e quote below is relatively long, it is important to understand Mr. Archer's decision and 727 strategies of presenting data holistically, which we argue indicated learning and the development of relational agency. Kevin Archer:  I don't know if it's important, but it is certainly interesting to me, and I think it might be interesting to those sitting around the table. I wanted to see what that looked like relative to a greater dip in history. What has been over the course of time, the volume of the ethnic makeup of the students who were expelled was interesting to me and I thought would be germane to the conversation. Here's what I know: I broke the data into three chunks. The last 10 years, 21 students have been expelled from our high school. I thought, okay, 21 students over 10 years, probably in the ballpark where other schools in our neighborhood would be if I asked principles of our and our neighbors. So not too terribly out of out of whack. Out of those 21 stude nts, there were nine students who were Native American students. 11 students who are white students and one African Americans student. Okay, so 42% to go by our percentages, we're talking 42% of our expulsions happen to Native American students, alright, in the last 10 years. Now, just for just for comparison’s sake, In the year 2000, alone, there were 21 expulsions. Facilitator 2:  In the year 2000? Kevin Archer:  Right. In the year 2000, there were 21 expulsions. So, from the year 2000 to 2009, 57 students were expelled; 35 Native American students; A 61% rate of expulsion being Native American students. You see where I'm going with this? Since the spreadsheet that was provided to me only went back to '94, I don't have 10 years in this next segment . But in the six years  starting in '94 going up to '99 there were 40 students expelled, so high rate right there too for just those six years. 40 students e xpelled: 22 Native American students, 15 white students. The rate for Native American expulsion was 55%. Gwenwyn:  What the heck was going on in 2000? That was the boulder boys that were coming together with the white shirts. It's  from one particular community. It was a group friends and it was their real racist viewpoint. And they were going to wear white shirts to school to show they're opposite of native. Jeremiah:  And then outside of school that group, some of them lived on the reservation burned down [local] village. In that era. It was a backlash of treaty rights. Here, we can see that Mr. Archer has demonstrated stronger growth in his relational agency. That is, he was able to recognize the historical legacies of systemic oppression embedded in school disciplinary practices. Mr. Archer joined the rest of ILL  members, particularly Ojibwe members, to ground and unearth the root causes of racial disproportionality in school discipline within the settler -colonial history of NHS and its community. With the transformed understanding of the socio- spatial-historical context of racial disproportionality in NHS, members advanced their collaborative work to design (i.e., model and examine) their ideal behavioral support system, which emphasized restoring the broken relationship between the school and the local Indigenous community. Discussion In this paper, we expanded Edwards’s original concept of relational agency and argued that in boundary-crossing efforts in the context of racialized and politicized U.S. schooling, relational agency needs to include one's ability to draw upon historical accounts and interpretations of systemic oppression and racism when working together to unpack the root causes of racial disproportionality in their localized contexts. This is the first step towards designing the new culturally responsive behavioral support  system. The case of Mr. Archer’s relational agency provides an example of how relational agency is possible when members, particularly those in power and privilege, were able to acknowledge the socio -spatial-historical contexts of racial disproportionality and center the perspectives of those who have been historically marginalized and utilized those perspectives for collective learning and growth. This paper can advance existing literature on relational agency, particularly within a co- design of an educational system and reform that requires collaborative boundary- crossing work. While relational agency is a familiar concept in the field of learning science, the framework proposed here can significantly contribute to addressing educational challenges within politicized and racialized contexts. This expanded framework holds value for researchers, practitioners, and decision-makers alike who are interested in conducting school reform that 728 centers the knowledge and lived experiences of historically marginalized members of the school and community to address complex educational problems at the local level. papers.title: Enacted Utopias for Transformative Agency, Survivance, and Sovereignty
papers.authors: Sovereignty Aydin Bal, Aaron Bird Bear, Aydin Bal, Aaron Bird Bear
papers.abstract: The United States of America has striven for the dissolution of Indigenous societies by establishing a colonial society on seized land, quelling sovereignty, and collective agency of Indigenous communities. This has disrupt ed Indigenous people’s ever -evolving, multilayered cultural-historical identities and future -making activities as transformative agents. Settler colonialism forced Indigenous people to assimilate into an ahistorical  existence of individual objects within the settler -native dyad through genocide,  resettlement, and education. In this paper, we will present a-four-year long formative intervention study, Indigenous Learning Lab, implemented at a rural high school serving an Anishinaabe tribal n ation in the state of Wisconsin. Indigenous Learning Lab facilitated transformative agency among American Indian students, families, educators, and community members and non-Indigenous educators to design and implement the school’s new behavioral support system. Genocide, resettlement, and education The United States of America (U.S.) was founded on settler colonialism, slavery, and land-based capitalism. U.S. has striven for the dissolution of Indigenous societies by establishing a colonial nation (Wolfe, 2006), quelling sovereignty and collective agency of Indigenous communities. This has disrupt ed Indigenous people’s ever - evolving, multilayered cultural-historical identities and future-making activities as transformative agents. Settler colonialism forced Indigenous people to assimilate into an ahistorical existence of individual objects within the iron cage of settler -native dyad through genocide,  resettlement, and education. In this paper, we will present a formative intervention study, Indigeno us Learning Lab, implemented at Northwoods High School through a coalition of an Anishinaabe  tribal n ation, Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction, Wisconsin Indian Education Association, and a university-based research team. The city where the school is located was the epicenter of Wisconsin’s Anti -Indian movement of the 1990s, the Walleye War. Anishinaabe  harvesters were physically attacked or prevented from practicing their treaty-guaranteed fishing rights on lands ceded in treaties.  The school had significant disparities in disciplinary actions. Indigenous students who made up 21% of the student population received over 60 % of the suspensions and 100 % of the expulsions in the 2014 -2015 academic year (U.S. Department of Education, 2018). The school leadership implemented Indigenous Learning Lab to further their partnership with the community and systematically address disparities  in behavioral outcomes : to move  beyond the status quo.  Indigenous Learning Lab aimed at facilitating transformative agency among American Indian students, families, educators, and community members and non- Indigenous educators to design the future of their school’s behavioral support system. Eight Indigenous community members (students, parents, teac hers, and a member  of the tribal government) worked with six non- Indigenous school staff and a research team including Indigenous and non - Indigenous scholars from a local university. Theoretical framework In this study, we utilize a cultural- historical activity theory -based transformative agency  and Freire’s (1971) liberation pedagogy. Transformative agency is a change- oriented process of undertaking actions to repurpose or expand the object of activity (e.g., from punishment to support) and create novel solutions to systemic contradictions (Engeström & Sannino, 2021). Freire (1993) stated When a word is deprived of its dimension of action, reflection automatically suffers as well; and the word is changed into idle chatter, into verbalism, into an alienated and alienating "blah." It becomes an empty word, one which cannot denounce the world,  for denunciation is impossible without a commitment to transform, and there is no transformation without action (p. 68). 1059 Infor med by the work of Spinoza, Hegel, Marx, Engels, Lenin, and other historical materialist philosophers, CHAT has three key ideas: The centrality of mediation, genetic (historical analysis), and grounding in culturally organized activity (Cole, 2015). Decolonizing agency in a settler colonialist system The settler colonialism in the U.S. took four institutionalized acts: Invasion, genocide, resettlement, and assimilation. U.S. cavalry captain Richard Henry Pratt, who opened the first boarding school in 1879 for Indigenous children in Carlisle, Pennsylvania in a speech summarized the purpose of the “ Kill the Indian in him and save the man.” Our historical analysis is informed by the decolonial approach: “Decolonization, as we know, is a historical process:  that is to say it cannot be understood, it cannot become intelligible nor clear to itself except in the exact measure that we can discern the movements which give it historical form and content” (Fanon, 1963, p. 36). Decolonization is not accountable to settlers’ expectations, interests, safety, and comforts and settler futurity, settler colonialism and its decolonization implicates and unsettles everyone ( Tuck & Yang, 2012). Two guiding principles of our decolonial approach to transformative agency is Indigenous sovereignty and futurity. Indigenous sovereignty is  the ability of Indigenous peoples and nations to unimpededly use Indigenous knowledge, languages, and ways of being to guide and shape how the Indigenous nations and people wish to be in this interconnected world.

papers.title: Elementary Students’ Emergent and Divergent Goals in Collective Embodied Modeling Activities
papers.authors: Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Joshua A. Danish
papers.abstract: This paper aims to understand how elementary students construct and pursue individual goals in a loosely structured collective embodied modeling activity. We explore how engaging in negotiating diverse goals impacts students’ sensemaking about an ecosystem  they are modeling. We used  Interaction Analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995) to discern students’ individual goals in their embodiment and communication and compared them to the collective goals stated by the facilitator and/or group strategies. Our findings lead to recommendations for educators and designers, emphasizing the importance of supporting students’ diverse goals to enhance their agency and foster a more inclusive learning environment.

papers.title: Cultivating Feedback Loops: Factors and Contradictions Impacting Groups Developing Emerging Technologies
papers.authors: Merijke Coenraad, Digital Promise Global, Judi Fusco, Pati Ruiz
papers.abstract: Feedback loops bring together participants from multiple contributing groups in purposeful, multi-directional, iterative, and transformative interactions to design or develop an innovation. We present the idea of three- way feedback loops between researchers, educators, and product teams. Using cultural-historical activity theory, we examine the cultural, historical, and contextual factors impacting each group’s  participation in a feedback loop and the contradictions that arise within and between the systems. As research increasingly aims to center the voices of individuals who are most impacted by its outcomes and ensure innovations best serve the communities for whom they are created, feedback loops are a promising collaboration strategy . However, cultivating a productive feedback loop requires careful navigation of the different contexts and the contradictions between the groups.

papers.title: Affect as Outcome: Centering Emotion and Equity in learning Sciences Research
papers.authors: Cynthia Carter Ching, Yeon Jade Lee, Tugce Aldemir, Ciara Thomas Murphy, Lee Martin, Marcela Borge, Erica Halverson, Tracey Bullington
papers.abstract: Our field often takes an instrumentalist approach to the role of affect in learning. This session examines the topic of emotions in learning environments, but we do not frame emotion as an antecedent or lever for engagement or motivation to learn. Rather, the papers in this session treat emotion as a critical outcome, and as a vital focus for research in and of itself . Whether the learning environments in question are designed or naturally occurring, the perspective and experience of learners takes center stage. Results across the collection of papers demonstrate that emotion is not only a critical factor to investigate in learning, but it can also be an equity issue as well, which makes it all the more worthy of attention in future research. Symposium theme and overview Learning scientists have recently been investigating the critical importance of emotion in learning, forwarding the role of phenomena like joy, pride, frustration, anxiety, grief, trust, affinity, dignity, righteous anger,  and others (e.g., Curnow, Fernandes, Dunphy, & Asher, 2021; Vakil & McKinney de Royston, 2019; Espinosa, Vossughi, Rose, & Poza, 2020). Other scholars have studied or designed technological tools to emphasize and scaffold socio- emotional learning (SEL) as a key component of collaboration, self-regulation, meta-cognition, and other aspects of school success (Farber, 2021; Zhang & Kaufman, 2017). Still other scholars have built models that go beyond an instrumentalist approach framing affec t as a catalyst or motivator for learning, and they have argued instead for emotion as a primary focus of study in and of itself ( Curnow & Vea, 2020). In this session, our collection of scholars and papers aims to push the conversation again, such that we acknowledge and investigate how emotion, on the one hand, can be  the primary goal  of the learning environments and opportunities we investigate and/or create, and on the other, can sometimes  override other goals to the extent that emotion ends up becoming the major result. In either case, we ignore affect-as-outcome at our peril. There are three frameworks in existing literature that support our approach and that we will use to frame this session. First is Mary Helen Immordino -Yang’s work on the biological basis of emotion and the role of emotion in learning, identifying the machinery through which experiences activate attention and become hardwired in memory (Immordino-Yang, Darling-Hammond, & Krone, 2019). Viewed through this lens, emotion is not just a lever or antecedent for learning; emotion  is learning (Immordino-Yang, 2016). Second, we look to Tanner Vea’s (2020) work on the learning of emotion as a sociocultural practice, as we situate learner emotion within institutions, activities, and communities housing a variety of learning environments and learning outcomes. Finally, third is Ruha Benjamin’s Race After Technology, which articulates how technologies and technological systems are inscribed with discriminatory mechanisms that privilege some groups and exclude or alienate others (Benjamin, 2019). Viewed through this lens, it is not surprising that we  often see learners and participants in our technology-infused projects experience a wide gamut of emotional responses as outcomes. Benjamin’s critical volume forces us to acknowledge that equity work in the learning sciences often cannot help but be emoti onal work, and vice versa, for our participants and for ourselves. Inequities of anxiety and distrust in undergraduates’ experiences with online proctored exams Yeon Jade Lee aand Cynthia Carter Ching Racialized mechanisms are embedded in video- based online exam proctoring technologies  in higher education, such as cases in which individuals with darker skin are less easily identifiable on video and thus more likely to be flagged for cheating (Yoder -Himes et al, 2022). Greater struggles with COVID -remote learning and assessment 1957 in high er education have also been associated with student family income inequality and digital inequality (Katz, Jordan, & Ognayova, 2021). While these findings provide a systems perspective  on the impacts of online exams, our goal was to investigate the lived experience of online exam proctoring from an individual student perspective. For this analysis, we focused in particular on the emotional load of preparing for and engaging in proctored exams. Frameworks We employ cultural-historical activity theory ( Engeström, 1993) to examine and articulate how the mandates of remote-proctored online exams shift the division of labor and the goal of creating cheat-proof environments from the university and the faculty on campus to the students and their homes. We also draw on the theory of racialized organizations (Ray, 2019) to describe how these shifts place a greater emotional and material burden on non- dominant and low -income students. Finally, we build on theories of  human cognition and human experience as inherently embodied (Nathan, 2021; Stoltz, 2015) to forward the importance of examining how emotion is related to the embodied experience of taking proctored online exams – a perspective that might seem less obvious, given a prevailing tendency within online learning and assessment research to focus on on- screen activity.

While there were challenges, o ur findings suggest that both researchers and teachers can benefit from collaborating . This pilot research is shaping future work to further bridge the gap between research and practice.
